stories.topic: Clean-bowling Rahul Dravid in office cricket
stories.summary: When Amit was managing editor at Cricinfo, Rahul Dravid visited the office. The staff played office cricket with a ball halfway between a squeezy ball and a plastic ball, which you could spin forwards or backwards to make it zip through the air. Amit persuaded Dravid to bat. His first ball was a wide, and then he clean-bowled Dravid with the next two. Dravid called him Shoaib Akhtar, refused to play on and threw the bat away.
stories.insight: Amit offers this as his entire 'action' record in cricket. It sets up the episode's premise: he is a spectator-analyst, not a practitioner, and is cheerfully honest about it.
stories.quote: My first ball was a wide. Didn't work out. He was clean bowled off the next two balls. And then he said, Fuck you, Shoaib Akhtar, I'm not playing with you. And he threw the bat away.

stories.topic: The cycling fan who can't ride a cycle
stories.summary: Ajay asks Amit for his 'thought to action ratio' in each sport. For poker it is high, since he played professionally for years. For cycling it is literally zero, because he never learned to ride. He grew up privileged (his father was in the IAS and there was always a car), and his working life in Bombay was local trains and buses until he bought a car.
stories.insight: Deep appreciation of a sport can be entirely intellectual. Ajay's line 'you don't have to be a hen to know about eggs' becomes the license for the whole episode.
stories.quote: And in cycles, it is literally zero because I don't know how to ride a cycle. Which I used to be very embarrassed about, but now I'm like whatever.

stories.topic: Oscar Pereiro, the accidental Tour de France champion
stories.summary: In a mid-2000s Tour (Amit doesn't recall the exact year), the favourites let a breakaway go that included Oscar Pereiro, who was not considered a serious contender. He gained enough time to lead for a while. The other contenders were busy fighting Floyd Landis and ignored him, so Pereiro finished second overall. Then Landis was disqualified for drug use, and Pereiro became Tour de France champion.
stories.insight: Letting a 'harmless' breakaway go is a calculated risk. When every rival is focused on one threat, the person nobody is watching can walk off with the prize, and luck can finish the job.
stories.quote: And all the other contenders were fighting with Floyd, so they completely ignored this guy. And after Floyd got disqualified, he became Tour de France champion.

stories.topic: Tour of Flanders 2022: Pogačar stalls himself out of the race
stories.summary: Tadej Pogačar (about 65 kg, a superb climber) attacked on the hills. Only Mathieu van der Poel (about 75 kg, a far better sprinter) managed to stay with him. Pogačar knew he could only win the sprint by coming out of Van der Poel's slipstream, so he refused to lead. Both slowed almost to a standstill, eyeing each other. Meanwhile three chasers, cooperating because they had nothing to lose, caught up. Van der Poel won, Dylan van Baarle was second, Valentin Madouas third, and Pogačar, the dominant rider all day, finished fourth.
stories.insight: Cat-and-mouse games have a hidden cost. While two rivals optimise against each other, third parties can catch up, and the cleverest move becomes self-defeating.
stories.quote: Pogačar ends up fourth because he waited too long and the other guys caught up and then he's the worst sprinter of the bunch.

stories.topic: Paris-Roubaix: Van Aert trapped by a two-man team
stories.summary: In last year's Paris-Roubaix, three riders were heading for the finish: the great rivals Mathieu van der Poel and Wout van Aert, plus Van der Poel's teammate Jasper Philipsen, a strong sprinter. Van der Poel attacked. Van Aert also punctured, so he had to chase with Philipsen sitting on his wheel. If he caught Van der Poel, Philipsen would beat him in the sprint; if he didn't, Van der Poel would win. Van der Poel won, Philipsen came out of Van Aert's slipstream to take second, and Van Aert was third.
stories.insight: Two teammates against one rival is a near-checkmate. Whatever the lone rider does, he spends his energy for someone else's benefit.
stories.quote: And the point is that Van Aert is fucked.

stories.topic: The 2023 Vuelta: the decoy who won
stories.summary: Jumbo-Visma had both Primož Roglič (who had won that year's Giro and three straight Vueltas) and Jonas Vingegaard (who had just won the Tour). They sent their star mountain domestique Sepp Kuss into a breakaway. The idea was to put him in the leader's jersey so that Remco Evenepoel's team would exhaust itself chasing him. Instead Evenepoel collapsed. Kuss now led with Roglič and Vingegaard second and third. Roglič wanted to race for the win, but there was outrage on social media: after years of helping others win, Kuss deserved a gift. Vingegaard was fine with that. The team let Kuss win and finished 1-2-3, and an angry Roglič left for Bora-Hansgrohe.
stories.insight: Team roles are fixed in theory but dynamic in practice. When the plan succeeds too well, loyalty, ambition and public sentiment collide, and the result can break a team.
stories.quote: then there is this outrage on social media and elsewhere that for years Sepp Kuss has helped you guys win all these things and this is one moment where you can gift him something beautiful.

stories.topic: Armstrong to Landis: 'Run like you stole something'
stories.summary: In what Amit recalls as Lance Armstrong's last Tour win, his domestique Floyd Landis paced him up the final mountain. Only four riders were left: Landis, Armstrong, Jan Ullrich and (Amit thinks) Ivan Basso. Having secured his time gains, Armstrong wanted Landis to take the stage and told him to 'run like you stole something.' The rivals wouldn't let Landis get away, so Armstrong said 'Fuck it, if he won't win, I will win' and took the stage himself.
stories.insight: Leaders do reward their domestiques, but only when the race allows it. The gift is conditional on tactics.
stories.quote: And Armstrong memorably tells Floyd Landis, run like you stole something because he wants Landis to win now.

stories.topic: Tour de France 2022: Pogačar against two Jumbo-Visma leaders
stories.summary: On a brutal mountain stage over the Col du Galibier to the Col du Granon, Jumbo-Visma put Wout van Aert in the breakaway so he could drop back and help their two leaders, Roglič and Vingegaard. Rivals didn't know Roglič was injured from an earlier crash. The front group thinned to Pogačar, Roglič, Vingegaard and a struggling Geraint Thomas. The two Jumbo riders attacked Pogačar in turn, and he had to close every gap. Then Pogačar launched his own attack. He failed to drop Vingegaard and burned so much energy that Vingegaard took about three minutes on the final climb and went on to win the Tour.
stories.insight: Even the strongest individual is in a bad spot against a coordinated pair. Some call Pogačar's attack stupid; Amit also floats the theory that he simply 'bonked', meaning he ran out of calories.
stories.quote: And then Pogačar does something which many people say is profoundly stupid. He decides, fuck it, I will attack and I will leave these guys.

stories.summary: Wout van Aert is so powerful that if he reaches the finish with a small group, he wins. So without any explicit collusion, rivals attack one after another and wait for him to chase, because chasing would cost them their own 'bullet.' The same used to happen to Peter Sagan. In the last Olympic road race, Van Aert, tired of chasing, let Richard Carapaz go. Nobody else chased either, and Carapaz took gold. Van Aert got silver and Pogačar bronze.
stories.insight: Being the clear favourite makes you everyone's target. Weaker rivals can tacitly coordinate to tire out the strongest rider, and the winner may simply be the attacker nobody bothered to follow.
stories.quote: It is just that he is the attacker who Van Aert chose not to follow. Because he was tired by then of following people.

stories.topic: Evenepoel, Van Aert and the Belgian team
stories.summary: At world championships and Olympics, riders race for national teams. A young Remco Evenepoel was told to work for Belgian favourite Wout van Aert. Van Aert didn't have the legs that day, and Evenepoel was furious, feeling he could have won. The next year Evenepoel broke away alone. Van Aert couldn't chase his own teammate and had to sit with the others, and Evenepoel won the world title.
stories.insight: Team obligations work in both directions. The same rules that once forced Evenepoel to sacrifice himself later stopped Van Aert from chasing him down.
stories.quote: And once he goes off on a breakaway, uh, you know, Wout van Aert cannot follow him because teammate.

stories.topic: Roglič: from skiing crash to cycling great
stories.summary: As a Slovenian teenager, Primož Roglič had a horrific crash at a junior skiing world championship, around 2007–08. Amit still rewatches the footage. Roglič skied again but realised he wouldn't be among the world's best, perhaps because the injury cost him a developmental phase, perhaps for mental reasons. He loved sport, so he took up cycling relatively late. Some say he's not a great bike handler because of that, yet he became one of the great riders of his generation and won the Vuelta three times.
stories.insight: A forced pivot, made late, can still lead to greatness when the underlying drive is intact.
stories.quote: But he says that I love sport, man. I just love sport. I want to go out there, I want to compete, I want to be physical. And he takes up cycling.

stories.topic: Tour 2020: the time trial that wasn't a collapse
stories.summary: In the Covid year, Roglič led the Tour going into the decisive second-last stage, a time trial. He was the current Olympic time trial champion and hadn't bothered attacking his 21-year-old compatriot Pogačar, who was about 30 seconds behind. As the last rider to start, Roglič heard radio updates that Pogačar had caught up with and then passed his time. On the final climb he looked close to tears, and his teammates, including Van Aert, knew the dream was over. Amit tweeted live that it was a seminal moment in world sport. Afterwards the 30-year-old Roglič hugged and congratulated Pogačar.
stories.insight: The popular story that 'Roglič collapsed' is false. He finished fifth out of about 150. Sometimes a loser didn't choke; the winner was simply extraordinary.
stories.quote: Roglič came fifth in the stage out of hundred and fifty people. He did a great time trial. But Pogačar was just on another fucking planet.

stories.topic: The doping arms race and the erased decade
stories.summary: Amit recalls that Greg LeMond, or possibly another top rider, took a few months off around the late 1980s and on returning could barely keep up because the pace had become absurdly high. Through the 1990s cycling became a drugs arms race, with EPO giving altitude-training-like effects. Tour winners from 1996 onwards (Riis, Ullrich, Pantani, Armstrong for seven years, then Landis, who was disqualified) were all on drugs. Rather than hand titles to runners-up, the authorities declared that the results of a whole period, including all seven of Armstrong's wins, don't count.
stories.insight: When everyone in a competitive system cheats, punishing one villain makes little sense. The honest fix is to void the era, and an outsider's return can be what reveals the new normal.
stories.quote: they took a few months off and then when they got back to the peloton, they could barely keep up with the peloton because the pace was so incredibly high and they realized something is fishy.

stories.topic: Van Aert's sacrifice, undone by a crash
stories.summary: Wout van Aert, also a cyclocross champion, skipped this year's cyclocross world championship so he could spend weeks at altitude preparing for the cobbled classics, the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix. As the cobbled monuments arrived, he crashed badly through no fault of his own and was out for weeks. Similarly, a crash at Liège-Bastogne-Liège last year disrupted Pogačar's preparation, and he couldn't truly compete at the Tour.
stories.insight: Elite preparation is now highly optimised, but it only improves your odds. One wheel touch can wipe out months of sacrifice.
stories.quote: Big sacrifice. And the moment he gets to the first big cobbled monument, Tour of Flanders, he has a terrible crash for no fault of his own, and he's been out since.

core_ideas.concept: You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay asks Amit for his 'thought to action ratio' in each sport, and for cycling it is zero. Ajay's line, which Amit credits to him, is that practice isn't required for understanding, and being inside the game can even get in the way of seeing it whole.
core_ideas.quote: You don't have to be a hen to know about eggs. In fact, being a hen is an impediment to knowing about eggs.

core_ideas.concept: A test of body and character
core_ideas.explanation: Unlike Formula One, where the car matters enormously, road cycling is one rider's body against another's on nearly identical machines. Over a three-week Grand Tour the toll shows on riders' faces, and the race becomes a test of character as much as fitness.
core_ideas.quote: by the time you're ending one of these grand tours, you can see it on the faces and their bodies, and it becomes a test of pure character.

core_ideas.concept: Slipstream: the physics that makes cycling a team sport
core_ideas.explanation: The lead rider cuts through the air and leaves a low-pressure pocket behind him. A rider tucked in that pocket saves about 30% of his effort. Almost every tactic follows from this: domestiques shielding leaders, breakaways rotating turns, sprinters hiding until the last moment, and time trials that space riders out so no one can draft.
core_ideas.quote: All the people that you see on the screen who are cycling are not putting in equal effort. It is the guys who are out on the wind who are putting in that effort, and the people behind them are not.

core_ideas.concept: Weight is destiny: climbers, punchers, sprinters, domestiques
core_ideas.explanation: Body weight, which a rider can control only partly, sorts riders into roles. Grand Tour winners are light climbers (around 61–65 kg) because power-to-weight dominates on long mountains. Heavier punchers (around 75–78 kg, such as Van Aert, Van der Poel and Sagan) have explosive power for flats, cobbles and short steep climbs, so they suit one-day classics. Sprinters save everything for the last stretch. Riders who don't excel at any of these often become domestiques, who work for the team's stars. Lance Armstrong was a heavier exception, but that was the doping era.
core_ideas.quote: If you are a lighter rider, you are likely to be a better climber. And to win a grand tour, by the way, you have to have a combination of different skills, but what is non-negotiable is climbing.

core_ideas.explanation: Road cycling has one-day classics (the five 'monuments' among them), time trials (one rider against the clock), one-week stage races and the three three-week Grand Tours. The monuments differ by terrain: Liège and Lombardia are hilly, Flanders and Roubaix are flat but cobbled and demand explosive power, and Milan-San Remo is flat until its late hills. Each format favours a different kind of rider.

core_ideas.concept: Different jerseys, different games on the same road
core_ideas.explanation: In a Grand Tour the general classification (the Tour's yellow jersey) goes to the lowest total time over three weeks. Separate competitions reward sprint points (green jersey), mountain points and the best young rider. A sprinter happily loses an hour on a mountain day because he is only chasing points, so riders around him may be playing completely different games.
core_ideas.quote: I will lose one hour on a particular stage. I don't give a shit. I just want to optimize for those stages where I can do well.

core_ideas.explanation: Early in a race a small group breaks away from the main bunch (the peloton). Teams that want to win the stage don't catch it immediately, or another breakaway forms and drains them. They hold the gap at around three minutes and time the catch for the closing kilometres. The peloton has an edge because a domestique told to ride flat out for only 20 km can go harder than breakaway riders who must last 100 km. Sprint teams sometimes play chicken, each refusing to chase so the other burns its riders, and the breakaway survives.
core_ideas.quote: Whereas a guy in the peloton who's a domestique would have been told, you are riding for twenty K. So you calibrate for twenty K

core_ideas.explanation: Strangers in a breakaway share the work silently, each taking a turn in the wind, because a lone rider can't stay away. Sitting in without working is 'desperately uncool', unless there is a tactical reason such as your team leader chasing behind. Near the finish the cooperation collapses: all else equal, the rider in front loses the sprint, so everyone slows and watches everyone else.
core_ideas.quote: Typically it is considered desperately uncool to be a cheater and only sit in the slipstream.

core_ideas.concept: Limited bullets: why two beats one
core_ideas.explanation: Every rider has only so many hard efforts, or 'bullets', in a race. When someone attacks, the others wait for someone else to chase so they can sit on his wheel. Two teammates can take turns attacking a lone rival, who must close every gap until he is empty. The same logic lets rivals wear down a dominant favourite without ever talking to each other.
core_ideas.quote: Because whoever spends energy chasing the first guy down will not have the energy to win in the end. You have limited bullets.

core_ideas.concept: Controlling a race with relentless pace (the Sky Train)
core_ideas.explanation: US Postal under Armstrong, and later Team Sky for Chris Froome, used domestiques to set a pace so high that nobody could attack. Rouleurs drove the flat sections, then mountain domestiques took over one by one until the peloton was strung out in a single line. Rivals lost their teammates while the team leader still had helpers.
core_ideas.quote: Beyond a certain pace, no one can jump away from you. The acceleration and power required is too much.

core_ideas.concept: Strategy before the race, tactics during it, run from the team car
core_ideas.explanation: Plans are set before a race, but a directeur sportif in the team car, with a TV feed and live power data, radios instructions as it unfolds. That includes reminding riders to eat, because 'bonking' (running out of calories) can end a campaign. Domestiques ferry food and drinks from the car to their leaders.
core_ideas.quote: So you have strategy, which you decide before a race, and then you have tactics which you decide during the race.

core_ideas.explanation: Dave Brailsford took British cycling from the bottom of the heap to Team Sky winning the Tour seven times in eight years. There was no single breakthrough. Instead the team looked for 1% improvements in diet, training plans, riding position, helmet aerodynamics and more, and let them add up. Amit teaches the idea to his writing students. Brailsford is now working to turn Manchester United around.
core_ideas.quote: His insight was you don't need one big improvement. You look at a bunch of different things, like what is your diet. What is your training plan? What is your position on the cycle? How aerodynamic is your helmet? And you improve one percent on each of them

core_ideas.concept: How doping was cleaned up: better testing and team incentives
core_ideas.explanation: From the late 1990s, doping was an arms race in which you had to dope just to compete. It ended because testing technology caught up and because teams, which suffer when a rider is caught, now monitor their own riders. Amit argues today's sport is by and large clean, and that today's high speeds come from better training science, such as altitude camps, so fans can watch in good faith.
core_ideas.quote: By and large, the riders are monitored by the teams for their own self-interest because they don't want one of the riders to be caught for drugs anymore.

core_ideas.explanation: One touched wheel can bring down a whole group, as when Vingegaard, Roglič and Evenepoel all crashed together at this year's Tour of the Basque Country weeks before the Tour. Teams try to keep their leaders near the front of the peloton to reduce the risk, but luck remains a huge factor.
core_ideas.quote: somebody's wheel touches somebody's wheel, and then there's a domino effect. So there's a lot of luck.

core_ideas.concept: We follow sport for its stories
core_ideas.explanation: The physical spectacle draws us in, but rivalries and redemption arcs keep us watching. Examples include Roglič's unfinished quest for the Tour, Pogačar against Vingegaard, the Belgian tension between Evenepoel and Van Aert, and the Van Aert versus Van der Poel rivalry that began in cyclocross.
core_ideas.quote: we follow sport not just to see the limits of human achievement, but we get caught up in the stories of the people who are involved. We care about key rivalries, we care about redemption tales, and those matter a great deal.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's opening jab: 'Amit, tell me, you look like a guy who would be very fast on a cycle.' Amit: 'This is really a low blow. And the Bengali in me does not appreciate this low blow.'
Amit on learning to drive late: 'I am now the best driver in Bombay. Because driving in Bombay is not about driving, it is about Bombay. But that is a subject for another episode.'
Right after the hen-and-eggs line about knowing a sport without playing it, the episode is christened: 'Welcome to a scrambled eggs episode on cycling.'
A running gag casts Ajay as a 'card-carrying physicist' and aeronautical engineer, invoked as Amit explains the physics of the slipstream.
Amit explaining a breakaway: 'In a sense, when it comes to mainstream economics, you are a breakaway, and the peloton is far, far, far behind you.'

Ajay claims childhood cycling glory: riding up a slope and round a curve with both hands off. Amit: had he been French or Belgian, 'the loss of economics could have been the gain of cycling.' Ajay: 'This is why economic development matters.'
Amit's VPN advisory: 'Young men watching this for porn, okay? Do not do that. It is sinful, save your energy for studying economics and physics and aeronautical engineering.'
Chris Horner's favourite verdict on bad team tactics, which Amit relishes: 'Knuckleheads.'
Cycling's vocabulary is largely French because the French were pioneers of European cycling: domestique, directeur sportif, puncheur, and rouleurs (who 'just roll through these flat stages').
Amit thinks the fitness brand Peloton takes its name from the cycling term for the main bunch of riders.
Amit compares cycling's clean-up to cricket: 'Just as there is no more match fixing in cricket, I would like to believe, after a dark age, it's a similar thing in cycling.'

Ajay recalls reading that professional basketball instruments players so coaches can see their live VO2 max and substitute tired players. Amit notes cycling has the data but you can't swap riders mid-race.
Alpe d'Huez, the iconic Tour de France mountaintop finish that 'really separates the great climbers from the not so great climbers.'
Visma | Lease a Bike's pointy, wind-tunnel-designed time-trial helmet this season caused a fuss among rival teams, an example of how time trials are largely a contest of aerodynamic science.

Dave Brailsford, architect of Team Sky's success, is now Jim Ratcliffe's right-hand man at Ineos, which has just bought Manchester United. Manchester United is Amit's other passion, and he believes Brailsford will turn it around.
